title: Who, Where, What Happens
bigQuestion: How do you know what a story is really about?

story.title: The Slow One and the Fast One
story.kicker: A very old tale. A hare who is fast. A tortoise who is slow. Guess who wins.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz reads to her class in Chicago. It is a very old tale. A hare can run fast. A tortoise walks slow. The hare laughs at the tortoise. So the tortoise says, "Let us race." The hare says yes.
The race starts. The hare zooms off. He is far ahead. He looks back. The tortoise is a tiny dot. The hare says, "I have time." He lies down under a tree. He falls asleep.
The tortoise does not stop. Step. Step. Step. She walks past the sleeping hare. She walks to the line. The hare wakes up. He runs as fast as he can. Too late. The tortoise wins.
The class talks about it. Jae says, "The hare was fast, but he took a nap." Ruby says, "The tortoise never quit." Ms. Ortiz smiles. "Now you know what the story is about," she says.
story.think: The hare is faster. Why did the tortoise win the race?

lessons.title: Who Is in the Story
lessons.mainIdea: The characters are the people or animals a story is about.
reading: Think about the race. A hare. A tortoise. They are the ones in the story. They talk. They run. They do things. We call them the *characters*.
A character can be a person. A character can be an animal. A character can even be a talking cup! If it does things in the story, it is a character.
When you open a book, ask, "Who is this about?" Look at the pictures. Look at the names. Find the characters first. Then the story makes sense.

words.d: a person or animal that the story is about

look.title: The Lost Mitten
look.text: Look at this story. A boy named Sam drops his red mitten in the snow. A small dog finds it. The dog runs after Sam. The dog drops the mitten at his feet. Sam laughs and says thank you.
look.prompt: Who are the characters in this story?

check.q: What is a character?
choices: A person or animal in the story
The last page of the book
check.why: A character is who the story is about. The hare and the tortoise are characters.

check.q: Can an animal be a character?
choices: Yes, if it does things in the story
Only if it is a dog
check.why: A character can be a person, an animal or even a talking cup. It just has to do things in the story.

check.q: What is a good first question when you open a book?
check.why: Finding the characters first helps the story make sense.

lessons.title: Where and When It Happens
lessons.mainIdea: The setting is where and when a story happens.
reading: The hare and the tortoise race on a road. It is a sunny day. There is a tree. The hare naps under it. The road, the day, the tree. That is the *setting*.
The setting is where a story happens. It is also when. A story can happen in a city. It can happen on the moon. It can happen at night or long ago.
The setting changes the story. Snow means cold. A dark forest means scary. Look at the pictures to find the setting. Ask, "Where are they? When is it?"

words.d: where and when a story happens

look.title: Same Story, New Place
look.text: Picture a girl looking for her cat. Now put her in a quiet farm at noon. Now put her in a big city at night, with buses and lights. Same girl. Same cat. But the story feels very different.
look.prompt: Which setting makes the story feel scarier? Why?

check.q: What is the setting of a story?
check.why: The setting is the place and the time of the story.

check.q: Where does the race in the tale happen?
choices: On a road on a sunny day
In a boat on the sea
check.why: The hare and the tortoise race on a road. It is sunny, and there is a tree.

check.q: A story is set in a dark forest. How will it feel?
check.why: The setting changes how a story feels. A dark forest feels scary.

lessons.title: What Happens
lessons.mainIdea: Events are the things that happen in a story, one after another.
reading: The race starts. The hare runs ahead. The hare takes a nap. The tortoise walks past. The tortoise wins. Each thing that happens is an *event*.
Events come in order. First one thing. Then the next. Then the next. If you mix them up, the story breaks. The hare cannot nap before the race starts!
When you read, keep a list in your head. What happened first? What happened next? What happened last? Those are the events.

words.d: one thing that happens in a story

look.title: Three Things Happen
look.text: Picture this. A girl plants a seed in a cup. She waters it every day. A tiny green leaf pokes up. Three things happened. Each one is an event. Each one comes after the last one.
look.prompt: What was the first event? What was the last one?

check.q: What is an event?
choices: One thing that happens in a story
check.why: An event is one thing that happens. The hare taking a nap is an event.

check.q: What happens after the hare takes a nap?
choices: The hare laughs at the tortoise
check.why: While the hare sleeps, the tortoise keeps walking and passes him.

check.q: Why do the events need to stay in order?
choices: Mixing them up breaks the story
check.why: Events happen one after another. The hare cannot nap before the race starts.

lessons.title: What a Character Wants
lessons.mainIdea: Every character wants something, and that want moves the story.
reading: The hare wants to win. The tortoise wants to win too. She also wants the hare to stop laughing at her. A *want* is what a character is trying to get.
Ask, "What does this character want?" Then watch what they do. The tortoise wants to win. So she keeps walking. She never stops. Her want tells you why she does it.
Every story has a want. A dog wants a bone. A girl wants a friend. A boy wants to fly a kite. The want makes the story go.

words.d: the thing a character is trying to get

look.title: Leo and the Kite
look.text: Leo runs across the park with a kite. It drags on the grass. He runs again. It flops. He runs into the wind this time. The kite lifts up. Leo shouts. Watch what Leo does again and again. It tells you what he wants.
look.prompt: What does Leo want? How do you know?

check.q: What does the tortoise want?
check.why: The tortoise wants to win. That is why she keeps walking.

check.q: How can you tell what a character wants?
choices: Watch what the character keeps doing
check.why: What a character does again and again shows what they want.

check.q: Why does the tortoise never stop walking?
check.why: Her want to win tells you why she keeps going.

lessons.title: How a Character Feels
lessons.mainIdea: Words and pictures show how a character feels.
reading: The hare laughs at the tortoise. He feels proud. He feels sure he will win. At the end, he loses. Now he feels surprised. Maybe a little sad. These are his *feelings*.
A book does not always say the feeling. It shows it. A big smile means happy. Tears mean sad. Stomping feet mean mad. Look at the face in the picture. Look at what the character says.
Feelings can change. The hare felt proud at the start. He felt shocked at the end. Ask, "How does the character feel now?" Ask it again later.

words.d: what a character feels inside, like happy, sad or mad

look.title: Look at Her Face
look.text: Picture a page in a book. A girl stands by a broken bike. Her mouth is turned down. Her arms hang low. She looks at the ground. The words only say, "Mia stood by her bike." But you know how she feels.
look.prompt: How does Mia feel? What in the picture tells you?

check.q: How does the hare feel at the start of the race?
check.why: The hare laughs at the tortoise. He is sure he will win.

check.q: A character stomps her feet. How does she likely feel?
check.why: Stomping feet is a way a book shows that a character is mad.

check.q: Can a character's feelings change in a story?
check.why: The hare felt proud at the start and shocked at the end. Feelings change.

lessons.title: The Problem and the Fix
lessons.mainIdea: Most stories have a problem, and the story shows how it gets solved.
reading: The tortoise has a *problem*. The hare is faster. How can she win? A problem is something that is wrong or hard for a character.
The story shows the fix. The tortoise keeps going. The hare naps. She passes him. The problem is solved. That is the *solution*. A solution is how the problem gets fixed.
Find the problem in every story. Then find the solution. Sam lost his mitten. The dog found it. Problem, then solution. Most stories work this way.

words.d: something that is wrong or hard for a character

look.title: The Stuck Ball
look.text: Look at the yard. A ball is stuck up in a tree. Two kids look up at it. They cannot reach. Then one kid gets a broom. She pokes the ball. It drops. Both kids cheer.
look.prompt: What was the problem? What was the solution?

check.q: What is the tortoise's problem?
choices: The hare is faster than she is
She does not like the road
check.why: The hare is faster. The tortoise must find a way to win anyway.

check.q: What is a solution?
choices: The way a problem gets fixed
check.why: The solution is how the problem is solved. The tortoise keeps going and wins.

check.q: The ball is stuck in a tree. The girl pokes it with a broom. What is that?
check.why: The stuck ball is the problem. Poking it down is the solution.

lessons.title: Tell It in Order
lessons.mainIdea: To retell a story, say the events in order: first, next, then, last.
reading: Close the book. Now tell the story. First, the hare laughs at the tortoise. Next, they race. Then the hare naps. Last, the tortoise wins. That is a *retelling*.
Use order words. First. Next. Then. Last. They keep the events in line. Say who the characters are. Say where it happens. Say the problem and the fix.
The pictures can help you. Flip through them. Each picture shows an event. Point to a picture. Say what happens. Move to the next one.

words.d: to tell a story again in your own words, in order

look.title: Pictures in a Picture Book
look.prompt: Use the pictures to retell the story. Which event comes third?

check.q: What are the order words?
check.why: First, next, then and last keep the events in order when you retell.

check.q: What happens first in the tale?
choices: The hare laughs at the tortoise
check.why: The story starts with the hare laughing. That is why the tortoise asks to race.

check.q: How can pictures help you retell?
check.why: Each picture shows one event. Point to each one and say what happens.

lessons.title: Ask Good Questions
lessons.mainIdea: Who, what, where, when and why questions help you understand a story.
reading: Who raced? The hare and the tortoise. Where? On a road. When? On a sunny day. What happened? The tortoise won. Why? The hare took a nap. These are the *question words*.
Who asks about the characters. Where and when ask about the setting. What asks about the events. Why asks for the reason. Every story can answer all five.
Ask them before you read. Ask them while you read. Ask them after. If you can answer all five, you understand the story.

words.d: who, what, where, when and why

look.title: Five Questions, One Story
look.text: Here is a tiny story. On Monday morning, Ana found a lost puppy at the park. She took it home because it was cold. Who? Ana. Where? The park. When? Monday morning. What? She found a puppy. Why did she take it home? It was cold.
look.prompt: Which question word asks about the setting?

check.q: Which question word asks about the characters?
check.why: Who asks about the people or animals in the story.

check.q: Why did the tortoise win the race?
check.why: The hare stopped and slept. The tortoise kept going and passed him.

check.q: Which question asks for a reason?
check.why: Why asks for the reason something happened.

lessons.title: Two Tales, One Lesson
lessons.mainIdea: Two versions of a tale can differ, but each story teaches a lesson.
reading: Ms. Ortiz reads a second book. This time the race is in a city. The hare rides a scooter. The tortoise walks. The hare stops for ice cream. The tortoise still wins.
Two books can tell the same tale. That is a *version*. The setting changed. The hare's nap became ice cream. But the characters, the problem and the ending stayed the same.
Both books teach the same *lesson*. Keep going and do not quit. A lesson is what the story wants you to learn. Ask, "What did the character learn?" That is the lesson.

words.d: one way of telling a tale that can be told many ways
what a story wants you to learn

look.title: Same Race, Two Books
look.text: Book one: a road, a tree, a nap. Book two: a city, a scooter, an ice cream stop. In both, the hare is faster. In both, the hare stops. In both, the slow one wins. Two versions. One lesson.
look.prompt: What is the same in both books? What is different?

check.q: What changed in the second version?
choices: The setting and the hare's stop
check.why: The city, the scooter and the ice cream are new. The tortoise still wins.

check.q: What is the lesson of the tale?
choices: Keep going and do not quit
check.why: The tortoise wins because she never stops. That is what the story wants you to learn.

check.q: How do you find the lesson of a story?
check.why: The lesson is what the character learns. Ask that question and you will find it.

review.q: Who are the characters in the old tale?
review.why: Characters are who the story is about. The hare and the tortoise race.

review.q: The race happens on a road on a sunny day. What is that?
review.why: The setting is where and when the story happens.
The hare is faster. She solves it by never stopping.

review.q: Which words help you retell in order?
review.why: Order words keep the events in line when you retell.

review.q: The hare laughs at the tortoise. How does he feel?
review.why: Laughing at the tortoise shows the hare feels proud and sure he will win.

review.q: The second book has a city and a scooter. What stayed the same?
review.why: Two versions can change the setting. Both teach: keep going and do not quit.
